passage:
At two, Mridul patted the teddy on the head, announced, "Teddy hungry," and held a spoon to its mouth. Then came a blanket and a whispered "Night night." The teddy went to bed, and Mridul tiptoed away.

At sixteen, Mridul told Abhinav, "My chatbot really gets me. It's the only one that listens." After an update the replies felt colder, and Mridul felt hurt, as if a friend had changed overnight. Abhinav said gently, "It writes words that sound caring. But I'm here and I'd like to hear about your day." Mridul was quiet, then agreed to talk.

At twenty, Mridul thumped the desk when the laptop froze. "It hates me. Every time I have a deadline." Thomas, a roommate, laughed and said the laptop wasn't out to get anyone. Mridul grinned and gave it a coaxing pat anyway. "Come on, old friend, just one more page."

qa.q: What did Mridul say the teddy was when patting its head at two?
What do the teddy, the chatbot and the laptop have in common, and how do they differ?
qa.a: At two, at sixteen and at twenty Mridul sees feelings or motives in something without a mind: the teddy is hungry, the chatbot gets me, the laptop hates me. At two this is care-practising play; at sixteen Mridul is hurt when the chatbot changes; at twenty it is a joking way to make the freezing laptop feel less random.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling after the update made the chatbot's replies colder?
qa.a: Mridul felt hurt and let down, as if a friend had changed overnight.

qa.q: What could Abhinav do to support Mridul beyond gentle words?
qa.a: Abhinav could spend time with Mridul in person and suggest talking to friends or family, so support comes from people as well as the chatbot. 🙂

grounding: A toddler feeding a teddy, a teen treating a chatbot as a caring friend and a young adult blaming the laptop show the mind seeing feelings and motives in things.
